newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl coalition in deepest crisis yet over budget.
newsitem.headline: Kohl coalition in deepest crisis yet over budget.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl faces the biggest crisis in his record 14 years in office as his hamstrung centre-right coalition draws repeated blanks in a desperate search for budget funds to enable Germany to qualify for the single European currency.

The latest dead-end appeared to have been reached on Tuesday when coalition sources said Bonn would back off from a controversial plan to force the Bundesbank to revalue its gold reserves to pay out an extra profit to help reduce state debt.

Two special leadership meetings among Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) and liberal Free Democrats (FDP) have so far failed to find other sources of revenue to plug gaping holes in the 1997 budget.

On top of all that, Kohl and Finance Minister Theo Waigel have come up against unprecedented grumbling within their own ranks as federal and state politicians looking ahead to next year's elections start worrying about voter backlash.
"The situation is more serious and difficult than it has ever been during the whole life of this government," said Alois Glueck, a key Waigel ally in the Bavarian state government.
The majority view in Bonn is that Kohl's coalition has no choice but to soldier on until the general election in September 1998.

But pundits and politicians feel the coalition has run out of steam and must be stumbling badly if it gets into an unprecedented row with the respected Bundesbank. Pollsters say public satisfaction with its work has also been steadily falling in recent months.
"The government is gambling away its credit at home and abroad," noted an editorial in the Handelsblatt business daily entitled simply "The Decline".
Meeting the Maastricht treaty's tough criteria, including a three percent deficit-to-GDP target, is the centrepiece of Kohl's political strategy.

But faith in Germany's ability to manage this is fading fast after the Bundesbank blasted Waigel's plan to revalue its gold and pay out the profits to a fund for old East German debt, thereby reducing debt servicing from his budget.
Waigel's own party, the CSU, has refused to give him room to manoeuvre by stubbornly opposing a weakening of the treaty's deficit target.

Kohl's junior coalition partners, the pro-business FDP, have vowed to block any attempt to raise taxes as a stopgap measure to fill Bonn's coffers this year, when states wanting to join Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) have to meet the target.

The grumbling in the ranks started last week with one CDU backbencher. But it picked up momentum on Monday when CSU leaders balked and CDU deputies from North Rhine-Westphalia, the largest voting block in the party, demanded Waigel give up his confrontation course against the Bundesbank.
Waigel struck a more conciliatory line on Monday after a stormy CSU leadership meeting in Munich.

At the session, Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber and Glueck, his parliamentary leader, told him he had to find a compromise with the powerful central bank on the gold question or face a huge loss of voters' trust next year, CSU officials said.

A hastily-arranged meeting between Waigel and Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer on Tuesday raised hopes for a compromise draft law on the bank's statutes allowing for a gold revaluation in consensus with the bank rather than against it.

That could save Waigel the embarrassment of losing the vote in parliament on the bill. Kohl has only five votes more than needed to pass the bill and several deputies in the CDU and FDP have hinted they could vote against it if the bank disapproved.
But a compromise with the Bundesbank would probably not let Waigel rake in half of the 20 billion marks ($12 billion) profit this year to ease his budget burden.
That leaves the option of higher petrol taxes, faster privatisation and deep spending cuts, none of which will be popular among voters just before an election year.
The FDP, which is fighting desperately to save its image as the tax-cutting party, is not the only voice against tax raises.

Christian Wulff, 37, the Lower Saxony state CDU leader seen as one of the party's leading younger figures, broke ranks with the Bonn leadership on Tuesday to say that Waigel's last hope would be a "huge threat" to the party's image.

"The situation is extraordinarily serious," said Wulff, a key barometer of grass-roots opinion because he faces a crucial poll next March against Gerhard Schroeder, the state premier who could become the Social Democrat (SPD) challenger to Kohl next year if he wins.

Pressed to reveal where he would cut spending, FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt said Bonn could slash aid to students, new mothers and retired farmers. He added, however, that these were "cutbacks that go beyond the imagination of German society".
